(5th) 145, Justice Moen gave the following summary of test for striking out a statement of claim (at pp.
150-151): 14 Here the application to strike is made under Rule 129(1)(b) and (d) of the Alberta Rules of Court.
That Rule states: 129.
(1) The court may at any stage of the proceedings order to be struck out or amended any pleading in the action, on the ground that …
(b) it is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or …
(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court, and may order the action to be stayed or dismissed or judgment to be entered accordingly.
15 The Court of Appeal in Excelsior Life Insurance Co. v.
Zurich Investments Ltd.
14 (CA) noted that a factually hopeless case can be said to be frivolous and vexatious (at para.
That would appear to be the basis of the Defendants' application.
16 I note that Rule 129(1) is permissive: the court may order pleadings be struck out or amended.
Even in the face of an apparently frivolous action, it is in the discretion of the court as to whether the action will be struck.
17 The test for striking any action under any of the paragraphs (a) to (d) of Rule 129 is that it is “plain and obvious” or “beyond doubt” that the action cannot succeed: Bianco v.
935074 Alberta Ltd., [2007] A.J.
No.
274, 2007 ABQB 150 (at para.
8 citing Hunt v.
Carey, [1990] 2 S.C.R.
959, ¶ 30, and Cerny v.
Canadian Industries Ltd.
The Defendants say that this test must be applied to an analysis of the Statement of Claim in light of the facts alleged in the affidavits before the Court.
The Defendants argue that allowing an action that “cannot succeed” to proceed would amount to an abuse of process: Bianco at para.
18 The Plaintiffs agree that this is the test to be applied.
19 A law suit may be struck when it is hopeless in point of fact and beyond doubt that it is hopeless: German v.
Major (1985), 39 Alta.
L.R.
2, ¶ 8 (CA); Estrin v.
Law Society (Alberta) (1995), 35 Alta.
L.R.
20 The courts have expressed the test in other ways.
An action should be heard unless the action was obviously and incontestably bad: Dyson v.
Attorney-General, [1911] 1 K.B.
410 at pp.

21 If there is a chance the plaintiff might succeed, in spite of the length, complexity or novelty of a matter, or the strength of the defences available, the plaintiff should be allowed to proceed with its case: Hunt v.
Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R.
959, ¶ 33, Decock v.
Alberta, [2000] A.J.
No.
419, 2000 ABCA 122, ¶ 68; Tottrup v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection), [2000] A.J.
No.
435, 2000 ABCA 121, ¶ 8, Adrian v.
Canada (Minister of Health), [2004] A.J.
No.
502, 2004 ABCA 149, ¶ 5; leave to appeal refused [2004] S.C.C.A.
No.
275; Arcand Estate v.
Imperial Oil Ltd., [2006] A.J.
No.
23, 2006 ABCA 13, ¶ 2, McElheran v.
Canada, [2006] A.J.
No.
22 Pleadings must be read generously and only struck if flaws cannot be corrected via amendment: Fullowka v.
Whitford (1996), 147 D.L.R.
(4th) 531, ¶ 34 (NWT C.A.), Decock v.
Alberta, 2000 ABCA 122, ¶ 107.
Striking Out Prayer For Relief In Andruchow (Trustee of) v.
Seniuk, 2005 ABQB 549, 2005 CarswellAlta 1003, 383 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 173; additional reasons at 2005 ABQB 780, 2005 CarswellAlta 1499, 383 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 184, Veit J. said, at p.
177: A prayer for relief can be struck out where the prayer for relates to a pleading that discloses no cause of action.
Applicable Principles In RK v.

GSG, 2024 ABKB 121, Justice Mah summarized the legal principles applicable to applications to strike out a statement of claim because it does not disclose a reasonable claim: [12] These Defendants proceed on the basis that the Statement of Claim discloses no reasonable claim against them: Rule 3.68(2)(b).
I summarize the applicable legal principles as follows: • No evidence is submitted on such an application: Rule 3.68(2)(b) & (3).

An application to strike for failure to disclose a cause of action is dealt with based on the pleadings: PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc, 2021 ABCA 16 para 69. • The test is stated as follows: A claim will be struck if it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action: R v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd, 2011 SCC 42 (CanLII), [2011] 3 SCR 45 (McLachlan CJ) at para 17, or as the Northwest Territories Court of Appeal states in Fullowka v Whitford, 1996 CanLII 10199 at para 36: The major rule is that a pleading will not be struck out for want of a cause of action unless the flaw is plain and obvious and beyond doubt. • There are limits to the principle that on a motion to strike the pleaded facts are taken as being true.

Facts that are manifestly incapable of being proven or that amount to mere speculation are not taken as being true: Operation Dismantle Inc v The Queen, 1985 CanLII 74 (SCC), [1985] 1 SCR 441 at p 455; Imperial Tobacco at para 22.

Further, bald assertions of misconduct (such as malice, fraud, and deceit) will not be accepted as being true without reasonable particulars of the allegations: Clark v Hunka, 2017 ABCA 346 at paras 31-32, Walton International Group Inc v Rockyview (Municipal District No 44), 2007 ABCA 21 at para 12
G H v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24 at para 58. • The pleadings are to be read generously.
If, on an initial reading, the pleading is capable of several interpretations, it should be given the interpretation that will support the pleading.

The Court should not artificially read pleadings in a way that leads to a fatal deficiency: Perpetual Energy at para at 74. • An application to strike a pleading on the basis that it does not disclose a cause of action is not an assessment of the merits of the claim.

If the claim is properly pleaded it should not be struck, even if the plaintiff cannot demonstrate at the time of the application that the claim can or will be proven: Gay v Alberta (Workers’ Compensation Board), 2023 ABCA 351 at para 13

Elder Advocates of Alberta Society v Alberta, 2019 ABCA 342 at para 95. • If the Statement of Claim is irregular because it does not plead specifics, a possible remedy is to order particulars, not strike the claim: Perpetual Energy at para 74.
If particulars would not cure the irregularity, it is appropriate to strike the claim without giving an opportunity to amend: Gay at para 14.
Justice Mah also said, at paragraph 31, that the fact that a Statement of Defence had been filed did not prohibit him from considering an application to strike a Statement of Claim.

Justice Mah said: [31] Since I am restricting myself to a review of the Statement of Claim and no other pleading and no evidence, I am not convinced that there is an immutable legal rule that prohibits me from considering a striking out application even though each of these Defendants filed a defence.
Moreover, each of these Defendants, to one or extent or another, pleaded in their respective Statement of Defence that the Statement of Claim disclosed no valid cause of action against them.
Multiple Attacks on the Pleadings In Ernst v.
EnCana Corp., 2014 ABQB 672, 2014 CarswellAlta 2089, 6 Alta.
L.R.

(6th) 233, Chief Justice Wittmann said, at paragraphs 21–23: 21 This is the second application brought by Alberta to strike portions of the Fresh Claim, and the third time Alberta has challenged Ernst's pleading.
The first application was brought pursuant to Rule 3.68(2)(c) and (d) to strike certain allegations on the basis that they were frivolous, irrelevant or improper, or constituted an abuse of process.
I dismissed that application for the reasons set out in the September 2013 Decision.
The present application is brought pursuant to Rule 3.68(2)(b) to strike the claim against Alberta in its entirety on the basis that the Fresh Claim discloses no reasonable claim.
22 There is no absolute rule governing the order in which a party may attack the opposing party's pleadings.
That said, it is usually most convenient to bring all attacks at the same time, and failure to do so may be the subject of a costs award: Alexander v Pacific Trans-Ocean Resources Ltd, [1993] A.J.
No.
142 (CA) at para 7.
23 I agree with Ernst's submission that multiple attacks on the same pleading should be discouraged.
At the same time, I acknowledge that there may be circumstances where there is an explanation for multiple attacks on a pleading.
A meritorious application to strike a pleading should not be rejected simply because another application for similar relief has already been brought.

In this case, I find it significant that Alberta's applications to strike portions of the Fresh Claim do not seek to strike identical portions of the Fresh Claim, and are brought pursuant to different subsections of Rule 3.68(2).
I therefore find this second application attacking Ernst's Fresh Claim is not an abuse of process.
However, I will consider whether this application could have been brought as part of Alberta's first application when deciding on costs of this application.

Alleging Ouster of Court's Jurisdiction Rule 129 does not refer specifically to situations where it is alleges [sic] that the court's jurisdicition has been ousted … It is appropriate, however, to apply under Rule 129 where the jurisdiction of the Court is challenged on the ground that another forum has exclusive jurisdiction …Young Estate v.
TransAlta Utilities Corp.
L.R.
189, per curiam.
In this case, it was alleged that court's jurisdiction over a matter had been ousted by an arbitration agreement.
Effect of Current Trends in Law If current trends in the law may support the claim, it should not be struck out.

A claim will not be struck out because it is contrary to current authorities, if an appeal to a higher court might succeed in overruling those authorities… And Wilson J. said that a claim should not be struck out if the trend of recent decisions suggests that the law is moving toward supporting such a claim and in a few years that may well be the law: Hunt v.
385]… I do not read that as repealing R.
129(1)(a), simply because in the 25th Century Buck Rogers will be able to do anything he wants.
But it does apply to foreseeable sorts of trends in the law.
Galand Estate v.
Stewart (1992), 6 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 399 (C.A.), at 408-409, per Côté J.A.
In Polsom v.
Couston, 2014 ABQB 43, 2014 CarswellAlta 252, 581 A.R.
342 (Master), the plaintiff alleged the tort of misfeasance in public office.

Master Hanebury said at paragraphs 3–6: 3 The case law has held that when considering an application to strike a claim, the court must proceed by assuming that the facts as found in the claim are true.
Only if it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot succeed should it be struck: Alberta v.
Elder Advocates of Alberta Society, 2011 SCC 24 at para 20; Odhavji Estate v.
Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69 at para 15; R. v.
Imperial Tobacco Canada Limited, 2011 SCC 42 at para 17; Donaldson v.
Feral, 2011 ABQB 11 at para 30.
At the same time, the Court should keep in mind that needless litigation should be avoided: Tottrup v.
Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2000 CarswellAlta 365 at para 9.
4 The fact that the law has not yet recognized the particular claim is not determinative.

Developing or novel areas of law are often not amenable to striking or summary judgment applications as they can require a full exploration of the facts: Persons with Developmental Disabilities, Edmonton Region Community Board v.
Pearl Villa Homes Ltd., 2010 ABQB 786; Shell v.
Barnsley et al., 2006 MBCA 133 at para 14; United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) v.
548311 Alberta Limited, 1998 ABCA 121 at para 17.
The approach is to be generous, erring on the side of permitting a novel or arguable claim to proceed to trial: Imperial Tobacco, supra at para 21; Lameman v.
Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 42; Anderson v.
Air Sprint Inc.
2005 ABCA 332 at para 9.

5 The law of the tort of misfeasance in public office is in a state of evolution, and the nature of this claim claim comes within the parameters of a developing area of law: Michael Bodner, “The Odhavji Decision: Old Ghosts and New Confusion in Canadian Courts”
(2005) 42 Alta L Rev.
6 Therefore, while the question to be determined is whether it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot succeed, the approach of the court to the pleadings should be generous.

Applicant's Pleadings Must Disclose Defect Relied Upon If a defendant intends to apply to strike out a statement of claim because of a failure on the part of the plaintiff to take some step required by law (e.g., give notice to the defendant under applicable legislation), then the defendant must either make the application to strike out the statement of claim before filing a statement of defence or the defendant must include in his or her statement of defence an allegation of the failure upon which the defendant intends to rely in the application to strike out. … if the appellant in the present case intended to rely on the failure to give notice at the time he filed his statement of defence he should have included it as part of his defence, or he should have brought on the present application before his defence was filed.
I do not, however, think that the failure to plead the section is of itself a waiver… The present appeal is, however, concerned with an application to strike out a statement of claim.
A defence has been filed without pleading the section which forms the basis for the application to strike out.
I think an amendment is necessary before the present application can succeed.
Strap v.
Canada (Administrator of Motor Vehicles Accident Claims Act), [1977] 1 W.W.R.
40 at 44 (Alta.
Limitation of Actions Defence The allegation by a defendant of a limitation defence most likely will not permit the court to strike or dismiss an action under R.
The chambers judge who heard this appeal dismissed it.
She agreed with the master that the appellant's claim was statute barred, and that it was doomed to fail.
Although she did not say so, she must have concluded that for these reasons, the claim was an abuse of the process of the court.

It appears from the reasons for judgment of the chambers judge that before her, counsel for the appellant questioned whether it was appropriate for the respondents to proceed on these grounds under R.
He relied on Western Industrial Contractors Ltd. v.
Sarcee Developments Ltd.
L.R.
In that case Mr.
Justice Virtue said at pp.

156 and 157: The Limitation of Actions Act may or may not provide a defence, but in any event it is a defence that must be pleaded and proved … The facts giving rise to this defence must be proved in evidence.
The passage of the time limited by the Act does not of itself remove the cause of action.

Accordingly, the existence of a defence under the Limitation of Actions Act is not a proper basis on which to strike out a statement of claim, particularly in a situation such as this where there are triable issues of fact and law to be resolved before it can be determined whether a defence under the Act exists or not.
In our view these comments apply to dismissal of an action, as well as to the striking of a statement of claim, under R.
Boudreault v.
Barrett (1995), 33 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 60 (C.A.), at 64, per curiam.

Splitting Applications Splitting the applications is undesirable but not impossible. … I do not see how an order to strike out one paragraph of a pleading can be said to be res judicata on an application to strike out another and different paragraph.

I agree that as a matter of general practice each party should be limited to one motion to strike out but there may be special circumstances under which a second motion may be made on proper terms as to costs.
Grassick v.
Calgary Power Co., [1947] 2 W.W.R.
749 (Alta.
C.A.), at 755, per O'Connor J.A.
In Canada Post Corp. v.
Goodfellas Delivery Inc., 2002 ABQB 585, 2002 CarswellAlta 1429, 322 A.R.
13, Rawlins J. noted that there is not an absolute prohibition against multiple applications to strike out pleadings.
At p.

21, her Ladyship said: A general statement of the law is, as the Appellant contends, that absent special circumstances, each party will be afforded only one opportunity to strike the other's pleadings: see Grassic v.
Calgary Power Co., [1948] 1 D.L.R.
103 at 106 (Alta.
This rule reflects a desire to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings which would unduly strain economic resources and require valuable court time.
In Horii v.
Canada (Attorney General), [2000] F.C.J.
No.
163 (T.D.), at para.
10, the Court stated that the rule derived from Grassic “is at least in part based on the principle that a litigant ought not to be faced with a continuing series of motions on similar subjects”.
The Respondent, on the other hand, points out that the rule in Grassic was revisited by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Alexander v.
Pacific Trans Ocean Resources, [1993] A.J.
No.
At page 3 [A.J.], the Court held: There are some authorities which either dictate, or seem to dictate, the order in which a party may attack his opponent's pleading or get particulars of it.
Some authorities even suggest that if one takes these steps in the wrong order one is debarred from relief which he could have otherwise have got.
When that is coupled with the Alberta custom of demanding particulars … that leaves many puzzles for counsel.
In our view, there are no such absolute rules and a party cannot become estopped in that manner.
We do not read Grassic v.
Calgary Power Co., [1948] 1 D.L.R.
103 (Alta.
C.A.) as saying any such thing.
Indeed, in our view, it is usually most convenient that a Defendant try to bring all such attacks about the same time.
Delay in doing so, or piece meal attacks, may be the subject of cost awards or even (in a closely-balanced case) a ground to refuse particulars.
(emphasis added) The rule in Grassic, therefore, should be seen as a general principal rather than as an absolute.

In fact, it seems likely that the Court in Grassic envisioned it this way since it considers, at 106, that “there may be special circumstances under which a second motion may be made on proper terms as to costs”.
Striking Third Party Notice The same considerations apply to striking out a third party notice as apply to striking out a statement of claim, where the application is under Rule 129(1)(a).
On an application to strike out a statement of claim the court looks only at the statement of claim.
Is it bad on the face of it?
In my view, on an application to strike out a third party notice it is necessary to look at the statement of claim as well as the third party notice.
By itself the third party notice may be difficult, if not impossible, to understand.
Rule 66(2) requires that a copy of the statement of claim be served with the third party notice.
For the purpose of an application of this nature the statement of claim must be looked at to place the third party issue in a proper context.
For the purpose of this application the allegations of fact both in the Statement of Claim and in the Third Party Notice must be taken as true.
Silliman Construction (Alberta) Ltd. v.
Johnson, Ming & Co.
407 at 409-10 (Master).
The Alberta Court of Appeal reversed this decision on other grounds [(1984)31 Alta.
L.R.
However, the comments of the master were not criticized.
Indeed at p.

287, the Court of Appeal said: “Assuming all factual allegations made in the … pleadings to date to be true …” In the view of Master Funduk: … a plaintiff can move to set aside a third party notice on the ground it does not disclose a case for contribution or indemnity.
That makes it an application under R.
The same considerations must apply to the application regardless whether the applicant be a plaintiff or a defendant.

To apply different considerations, or additional considerations, depending on who the applicant is, would be to relegate a plaintiff to an inferior status, which would not be consonant with the status given a plaintiff by R.
The issue whether a pleading discloses a cause of action must be decided from the fact of the pleading itself.
A third party notice does not stand on its own, because it is solely a claim over by defendant.
Consequently, the third party notice cannot be considered in isolation.
Resort must be had to what precedes it in the action.
For the purpose of an application under R.
129(1)(a) the allegations of fact in the impugned pleading are assumed to be true.
However, if the allegations of fact in the preceding pleadings are also assumed to be true there can be difficulties.

If the allegations of fact in both a statement of claim and a statement of defence are assumed to be true there cannot be a resolution of the status of the third party notice because the allegations of fact in the statement of claim and in the statement of defence are invariably in conflict.
In my view, the proper approach to an application to set aside a third party notice is to proceed on the basis
(a) the plaintiff will be successful in obtaining judgment against the defendant on the cause of action advanced in the statement of claim, and
(b) the allegations of fact in the third party notice are true.

The question then becomes, if the plaintiff is successful in establishing the cause of action he advances against the defendant does the third party notice disclose, on its face, a right to claim over against the third party?
This means the claim over must be measured in relation to the plaintiff's claim.
Indeed, the concept of contribution or indemnity exists only in relation to a defendant's liability to a plaintiff.
Without that liability there can be no contribution or indemnity.
Viewed in that light, it means the statement of defence does not play a part in this application.
There is no inequity in that.
A statement of defence goes to the merits of the plaintiff's claim.
The merits of any claims advanced in an action, be they claims by a plaintiff, by a defendant or by a third party, have no place in an application under R.
The merits of a plaintiff's claim are not considered.
The merits of a defendant's claim over are not considered.
The merits of a defendant's defence are not considered.
Westlands Industrial Park Ltd. v.
Burgee Developments Ltd.
L.R.
Assumption when Applying to Strike Third Party Notice The applicant, Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta applies for an order pursuant to R.
129(1)(a) of the Rules of Court to strike out the third party notice the defendants Sunshine Village Corporation, Michael Brett Klein and Peter Michael Kauffmann … On an application under R.
129(1)(a) no evidence is admissible; only the pleadings can be looked at.
Rule 129(2) provides: (2) no evidence shall be admissible on an application under clause (a) or subrule (1).
The facts alleged in the statement of claim are assumed to be true.
A further necessary assumption made is that the plaintiffs will be successful in their action.
The question then becomes, assuming that the facts alleged in the third party notice are true, does the notice disclose a claim which is within s.
17(3)(b) of the Judicature Act, R.S.A.

J-1, which provides: (3) The Court may grant to a defendant respecting an equitable estate or right or other matter of equity and also respecting a legal estate, right or title claimed or asserted by him.

(b) all such relief relating to or connected with the original subject of the proceeding and in like manner claimed against any other person, whether already a party to the same proceeding or not, who has been served with notice in writing of the claim pursuant to this Act or an order of the Court, that might properly have been granted against that person if he had been a defendant to a proceeding instituted by the same defendant for the like purpose, and a person served with the notice shall thenceforth be deemed a party to the proceeding with the same rights in respect of the defence against the claim as if he had been sued in the ordinary way by the defendant.
Gutek v.
Sunshine Village Corp.
L.R.
(2d) 116 (Q.B.), at 118, per Chrumka J.
Defence in Law, Defence in Fact, and Reasonable Defence To strike out [under the Rule] the statement of defence must not disclose a defence in law.
One cannot, under this rule, strike out a statement of defence merely because it is felt the defendant does not have a defence in fact.
The Rule provides that a defence can be struck out if it discloses no defence.
This is not to be confused with not disclosing a reasonable defence.
Ainge v.
DeCouteau (1980), 13 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 193 at 194 (Master).
Factually “Hopeless” Cases In German v.
Major (1985), 39 Alta L.R.
(2d) 270 (C.A.), Kerans J.A., speaking for the court, said at p.
274: Major asserts and I agree that the rule also applies in a case where the plaintiff's suit is hopeless in point of fact.
I hasten to add that I accept, on the authority of Cerny v.
Can.
Indust.
88 (Alta.
C.A.), that the rule in no case should be invoked “… unless the question is beyond doubt”.
At p.
276, his Lordship said: I agree that the test on invocation of that part of R.
129 [no cause of action] is: assuming the facts alleged in the claim are true, do they disclose a cause of action known to law?
When the question is, rather, whether the plaintiff's case is hopeless on the facts, the right question is that posed by Le Dain J.
(as he then was) in [Dowson v.
R.
C.A.)], at p.
138: is it “plain and obvious that the action cannot succeed”?

The distinction between applications to strike based on an allegation that no cause of action exists at law and those based on an allegation that the case is hopeless on the facts was again noted by the Court of Appeal: The Alberta Court of Appeal in German v.
Major[(1985), 39 Alta.
L.R.

(2d) 270 (C.A.)] stressed that where the defendant suggests that there is no such cause of action known to the law, i.e., that the plaintiff's lawsuit is bad in law or the defendant has a clear legal defence, then the court must assume the truth of the facts in the statement of claim.
But the Court of Appeal said it was different where the defendants contend that the lawsuit is hopeless factually, and thus frivolous and vexatious.
The test is whether it is “plain and obvious that the action cannot succeed.”Zurich Investments Ltd. v.
Excelsior Life Insurance Co.
L.R.
In Estrin v.
Law Society (Alberta) (1995), 35 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 153 (C.A.), the court commented on “hopeless” cases.
At p.
157 the court said: The case will not be hopeless in point of fact where plaintiff can point to some evidence to support the essential allegations of fact.
In Temilini v.
Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner (1990), 73 O.R.
(2d) 664 (C.A.), Grange J.A. drew the following distinction at p.

670: … I concede that the plaintiff should not enter litigation purely on a ‘fishing expedition’ but the distinction between that and using the processes such as production or discovery to supplement a case already based on some evidence is a fine one.
It is sufficient to say that a plaintiff who asserts a proper cause of action where there is some evidence upon which the case can be built should not be foreclosed.
If the Action Will Be Tried in Any Event The court should be loath to strike out a portion of a claim where the matter is to go to trial in any case.
In Sentinel Review Co. v.
Robinson, [1927] 2 D.L.R.
60, at p.

63 Meredith, C.J.C.P., overturned a Master who had struck certain portions of a defence using these words: It is manifestly better, when it can be done without prejudice to the interests of either party, that all questions in one action should be considered at one time by one court, thereby avoiding possible conflict of opinion and certain delay and needless costs.

Where a pleading is manifestly bad and is embarrassing, an officer at Chambers, as well as a judge at Chambers, has power to strike out the pleading, but, it should not be necessary to add, that powers should be exercised only in plain cases.
There is always some danger of a pruner cutting off a fruitful bough mistaking it for an unfruitful one.
Lamont, J., in Canadian Grain Co. v.

690 expresses a similar sentiment: Where, however, as here, after striking out the paragraphs which may be properly struck out, the plaintiff has to go to trial to prove his entire case, I do not see that any good purpose would be served by striking out any of these paragraphs.
I agree with the remarks of Ritchie, J., in Holmes v.

Taylor, supra, where he said: ‘If the cause is to go to trial, it had better go with the defence unmutilated.’ This rule was never intended to afford the plaintiff the opportunity of trying the case piecemeal.
The object of the rule was to prevent the delay and expense of an unreal defence.

I do not wish to be understood as holding that under no circumstances should a portion of a defence be struck out, but, generally speaking, but little will be gained by striking out an individual paragraph where the plaintiff has to go to court to prove his case.
If he has material sufficient to justify a court in striking out the paragraph it will usually be found sufficient to establish his allegation at the trial.
At any rate, the rules relating to admissions of facts for use at the trial afford the plaintiff ample protection.
In essence I must be satisfied that striking the offending paragraphs in no way imperils the statement of claim as a whole.
Murphy v.
Kenting Drilling Co.
77 (Master), at pp.
79-80, per Master Waller.
Master Waller's statement that “the court should be loathe to strike out a portion of a claim where the matter is to go to trial in any case” was quoted with approval by Russell, J.A. in Decock v.
Alberta, 2000 ABCA 122, 2000 CarswellAlta 384, 255 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 11; leave to appeal allowed (2000) 293 A.R.
388 (note) (S.C.C.), at p.
260 (notice of discontinuance filed September 10, 2001).
Rule Applies to Provincial Court I should mention that it was argued by the plaintiff that a judge of the Provincial Court of Alberta has no inherent power to strike out pleadings However, s.
19.1(2) of the Provincial Court Act provides that:

(2) Where this Act or the regulations do not provide for a specific practice or procedure of the court that is necessary to ensure an expeditious and inexpensive resolution of a matter before the Court, the Court may
(a) apply the Alberta Rules of Court, and
(b) modify the Alberta Rules of Court as needed.
Therefore, I find that the Provincial Court Judge had jurisdiction to strike out the pleading.
Parker v.
Menzies Field Mechanical Services Ltd.
204 (Q.B.), at 208, per Coutu J.
Standard of Review on Appeal From an Old Rule 129 (current Rule 3.68) Order Decisions on applications to strike are owed a high level of deference by this court.
Orders made under rule 129 are discretionary and appellate courts should only reverse if “it is obvious without elaborate argument that there is no cause of action”: Kvaerner Enviropower Inc. v.
Tanar Industries Ltd. et al.
The scope of review for decisions under rule 129 is limited to a determination whether:
(i) the decision was unreasonable because no weight or insufficient weight was given to relevant considerations; or
(ii) the chambers judge erred in law: Decock et al. v.
Alberta et al.
First Mortgage Alberta Fund (V) Inc. et al. v.
Boychuk et al.
1 (C.A.) at 3-4, per curiam.

Significant Deficiencies in Claims
